name: Einstein-Rosen Cylindrical Gravitational Waves
description: Exact vacuum solutions describing gravitational waves with cylindrical wave fronts and a single polarisation, converging on an axis, passing through it and spreading out again. Einstein's equations for them reduce to the flat cylindrical wave equation for one function and a quadrature for a second.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Guido Beck, working in Vienna, found the cylindrical gravitational waves in 1925 [beck1925, bicak2000]. He started from the static axisymmetric fields of Hermann Weyl and saw that the complex change of coordinates $z \to it$, $t \to iz$ carries them into fields that depend on time and describe cylindrical waves, and wrote down their field equations [bicak2000]. The paper went unnoticed in relativity [kennefick2005]. The waves carry the names of Albert Einstein and Nathan Rosen, who found them again in 1937 and noticed that they carry energy away from a mass on the axis [einstein1937, bicak2000].¶Einstein and Rosen concluded in 1936 that plane gravitational waves do not exist, since they could not avoid singularities in the metric [kennefick2005]. Howard Percy Robertson, as the anonymous referee of their paper, showed that the singularity was an artefact of the coordinates, which placed it on the axis of a cylindrical wave: with his change of coordinates "the worrisome singularities were relegated to the central axis of the spacetime" [kennefick2005]. The paper appeared in 1937 as "On gravitational waves", describing cylindrical waves [einstein1937, kennefick2005].¶At the conference in Bern in July 1955 Rosen reported that the pseudotensors of Einstein and of Lev Landau and Evgeny Lifshitz, computed in cylindrical coordinates, each give zero energy to the cylindrical waves of his 1937 paper with Einstein [rosen1956, kennefick1999]. Joseph Weber and John Wheeler took up that result in 1957, for a monochromatic wave or a pulse that moves in toward the axis through empty space, implodes on it and moves out again [weber1957]. They called it "the only problem of gravitational radiation where one has an accurate solution of the field equations of general relativity", and explained many of its "apparently paradoxical properties" by the analogy between gravitational and electromagnetic waves and by the equivalence principle [weber1957]. William Bonnor found the same year an exact cylindrical wave free of singularities everywhere, which comes in from $\rho = \infty$ at $t = -\infty$, reaches its peak near the axis about $t = 0$, and goes out to $\rho = \infty$ again [bonnor1957]. It is flat at spatial infinity and at $t = \pm\infty$, though not at $z = \pm\infty$ [bonnor1957]. Rosen found in 1958 that in Cartesian coordinates the energy and momentum densities of the waves are nonzero [rosen1958, virbhadra1995].¶Kip Thorne defined in 1965 an energy for systems that are unchanged by rotations about an axis and translations along it, which he called C-energy, a vector $P^i$ obeying $P^i{}_{;i} = 0$ whose component along an observer's world line is the C-energy density that observer measures [thorne1965]. Near the axis of a static system its density reduces to the proper mass density, and Einstein-Rosen waves carry it [thorne1965]. Far from the axis the metric on the plane of $t$ and $\rho$ tends to $e^{2\gamma_0}(-dt^2 + d\rho^2)$ with $\psi \to 0$, where the constant $\gamma_0$ is positive for any nonzero initial data of compact support, so space has a conical singularity at spatial infinity [bicak2000]. That conical singularity is "radiated out" to null infinity, by a relation that plays the part, in three dimensions, of Hermann Bondi's formula for the loss of mass [bicak2000]. Abhay Ashtekar and Madhavan Varadarajan showed in 1994 that the energy per unit length of such waves, the generator of time translations, is bounded from above, "a genuinely non-perturbative result", and that it agrees with the C-energy in weak fields and differs from it significantly in strong ones [ashtekar1994].¶The news function and the mass aspect carry over to cylindrical waves with both polarisations, as John Stachel showed in 1966, and the mass per unit length always decreases if there is any cylindrical news [stachel1966]. A second function $\omega$ in $e^{2\psi}(dz + \omega\,d\phi)^2$ carries the second polarisation, which Jürgen Ehlers (1960) and Alexander Kompaneets (1958) found independently [bicak2000, jordan1960, kompaneets1958]. Tsvi Piran, Pedro Safier, and Richard Stark evolved waves of both polarisations numerically in 1985, and found the usual cylindrical reflections together with a rotation of the polarisation vector wherever the second polarisation is present [piran1985]. Beverly Berger, Piotr Chruściel, and Vincent Moncrief proved in 1995 that asymptotically flat, cylindrically symmetric spacetimes satisfying the energy conditions hold no compact trapped surfaces, and that strong cosmic censorship holds among the electrovacuum ones [berger1995]. Vacuum spacetimes with a translational symmetry, the Einstein-Rosen waves among them, fail to be asymptotically flat in four dimensions and can admit a regular completion at null infinity in three, as Ashtekar, Jiří Bičák, and Bernd Schmidt found in 1997 [ashtekar1997].¶The Einstein-Rosen waves were the first radiative solutions of the field equations to be quantized, by Karel Kuchař in 1971 [bicak2000, kuchar1971]. He used the canonical methods of Paul Dirac and of Richard Arnowitt, Stanley Deser, and Charles Misner, and took the Einstein-Rosen time and cylindrical radius as canonical coordinates, conjugate to the density and the flux of C-energy [kuchar1971]. He proved their canonical formalism identical with that of cylindrical massless scalar waves in Minkowski spacetime, from which the identity of the two quantum theories follows [kuchar1971]. Ashtekar and Monica Pierri quantized the waves again in 1996, from the one to one correspondence between the Einstein-Rosen solutions and three dimensional general relativity coupled to an axisymmetric massless scalar field [ashtekar1996].

related.text: Exact gravitational waves with plane fronts. Einstein and Rosen concluded in 1936 that plane waves could not exist, since they could not avoid singularities in the metric [kennefick2005].

The wave that stands still, $\psi \propto \ln\rho$, the field of a line of mass [levicivita1919]. Guido Beck found the cylindrical waves in 1925 by the change $z \to it$, $t \to iz$ in Weyl's static fields [beck1925, bicak2000].

These waves closed up into a universe. Robert Gowdy changed their boundary conditions in 1971 [gowdy1971], and his $S^3$ and $S^2 \times S^1$ universes transform locally into an Einstein-Rosen wave wherever the gradient of the orbit area is spacelike [gowdy2014].

coordinates.name: Cylindrical

parameters.description: Wave amplitude, a dimensionless function of $t$ and $\rho$, with $e^{2\psi} = g_{zz}$; the spacetime is a vacuum exactly where it solves the flat cylindrical wave equation $\partial_\rho^2\psi + \partial_\rho\psi/\rho - \partial_t^2\psi = 0$ and $\gamma$ solves the two equations beside it; the pulse of Weber, Wheeler, and Bonnor, of width $a$ and amplitude $C$, is $\psi = \sqrt{2}\,C\sqrt{D_+ + a^2 + \rho^2 - c^2t^2}/D_+$ with $D_+^2 = (a^2 + \rho^2 - c^2t^2)^2 + 4a^2c^2t^2$

Dimensionless function of $t$ and $\rho$ fixed by $\psi$ through $\partial_\rho\gamma = \rho\left(\left(\partial_\rho\psi\right)^2 + \left(\partial_t\psi\right)^2\right)$ and $\partial_t\gamma = 2\rho\,\partial_\rho\psi\,\partial_t\psi$, and zero on a regular axis

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \rho, \phi, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, $\rho$ a length fixed by $g_{\phi\phi}\,g_{zz} = \rho^2$, and $z$ a length along the axis. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, so $\partial_t\psi = c^{-1}\partial\psi/\partial t$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Null

parameters.description: Wave amplitude, a dimensionless function of $u$ and $v$, with $e^{2\psi} = g_{zz}$; the spacetime is a vacuum exactly where it solves the flat cylindrical wave equation $2(v - u)\,\partial_u\partial_v\psi = \partial_v\psi - \partial_u\psi$ and $\gamma$ solves the two equations beside it

Dimensionless function of $u$ and $v$ fixed by $\psi$ through $\partial_u\gamma = -(v - u)\left(\partial_u\psi\right)^2$ and $\partial_v\gamma = (v - u)\left(\partial_v\psi\right)^2$, and zero on a regular axis

coordinates.convention: We use the retarded coordinate $u = ct - \rho$ and the advanced coordinate $v = ct + \rho$ of the cylindrical chart, both lengths, and $z$ a length along the axis. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
